title: Cristaux (1970). Gribouillis et calculs divers : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page is purely combinatorial. It shows a lattice diagram on squared paper (horizontal axis 1..18, vertical axis 1..16), two long, nearly parallel lines with dots at the lattice points along them, and a fan of lines drawn from the right-hand axis. Down the margins is a long list of comparisons between pairs of fractions.

At top left Grothendieck writes n/17 and then groups the values of n into classes: n=1,2,3; n=4; n=5; n=6; n=7,...,13; n=14; n=15,16. Each class has a small sketch of a convex broken line (two or three segments) beside it, and a column headed ν carries the values 1,2,3,1,2,3,2.

Most of the marginal inequalities pair n/17 with a nearby fraction of smaller denominator:
- 1/6<3/17, 1/9<2/17, 4/17<1/4, 2/7<5/17, 5/12>7/17;
- 2/3>11/17, 7/10<12/17, 3/4<13/17, 13/17<10/13.
In almost every case the two fractions are Farey neighbours, that is |17p - nq| = 1. For example 3·6 - 17 = 1, 2·9 - 17 = 1, 17 - 16 = 1, 35 - 34 = 1, 85 - 84 = 1, 34 - 33 = 1, 120 - 119 = 1, 52 - 51 = 1, 170 - 169 = 1. The exception is 4/5<14/17, where the difference is 2.

Similar comparisons appear for other denominators, which can be read as other heights h:
- denominator 23: 4/13>7/23, 1/3>7/23, 2/3>15/23, 3/5<14/23;
- denominator 24: 3/10>7/24, 2/7<7/24;
- denominator 18: 5/7, 10/14 against 13/18.

Interpretation, given the dossier 'Cristaux (1970)': this is the combinatorics of Newton polygons of F-crystals or Dieudonné modules. Take an isoclinic module of height 17 and dimension n, with slope n/17 and gcd(n,17)=1. Its Newton polygon is the segment from (0,0) to (17,n), which contains no interior lattice points. The polygons immediately adjacent to it in the specialization order (Grothendieck's specialization theorem, 1970) have a break point at the lattice point closest to the segment. That point is given by the Farey neighbours of n/17, i.e. the convergents of its continued fraction.

Grothendieck is computing these neighbours for each n, drawing the resulting polygons, and sorting the n by the shape of the adjacent polygons. The column ν plausibly records a count attached to each class, such as the number of segments or of break points. This is exploratory work toward understanding which polygons can occur under specialization, in support of the specialization theorem and the converse conjecture. The figure itself sketches lines of slope n/17 against the lattice in order to locate the nearest lattice points.
errors: '11/17 > 15/23' is false (11/17 ≈ 0.647 < 15/23 ≈ 0.652). In the image the sign appears to be crossed out, so Grothendieck probably caught the error himself.
Some correct inequalities have their signs struck through, e.g. 4/17 < 1/4 and 5/7 < 13/18. This suggests the signs were first written wrongly and then corrected; it is not a substantive error.
4/5 < 14/17 is correct, but these two are not Farey neighbours (difference 2), unlike most other pairs on the page.

ideas.what: Locating the lattice points nearest to the segment from (0,0) to (h,d) via Farey neighbours / continued fractions of d/h, in order to find the Newton polygons adjacent to an isoclinic one.
ideas.modern_name: Newton polygon strata; poset of Newton polygons and its covering relations (codimension-one jumps)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Specialization theorem: Grothendieck (1970), Katz (1979). Converse and the combinatorics of strata: Oort (Annals 2000; 'Newton polygon strata in the moduli of p-divisible groups'), de Jong–Oort (purity).
ideas.where_published: Specialization theorem and converse conjecture in Grothendieck's 1970 letter to Barsotti and in 'Groupes de Barsotti–Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné' (Montréal 1970, publ. 1974). The explicit Farey-neighbour computations are unsure/unpublished.

ideas.what: Case classification of n (mod 17) by the shape of the adjacent polygons (column ν).
ideas.modern_name: Combinatorics of the Newton polygon poset for a fixed height
ideas.usually_credited_to: Oort; later combinatorial work on Newton polygon posets (e.g. dimension formulas via lattice points under the polygon)

deep.surprise_reason: These are scratch computations: Farey neighbours of n/17 and n/23, and sketches of nearby lattice polygons. They fit Grothendieck's known 1970 work on specialization of Newton polygons. The underlying combinatorics was later systematized by Oort and others. Nothing here appears to be a finished or uncredited result.
transcription_corrections: '7/9 < 7/6' is likely misread; the right-hand fraction is unclear (possibly 7/8).
The bottom-right comparison is '7/10 < 12/17' (Farey neighbours); the '0' could also be read as '6', but 7/10 is the coherent reading.
'11/17 > 15/23': the '>' appears crossed out in the image.
'[-1/4-] ? 2/7 < 7/24': the struck-through item before 2/7 is an illegible scribble.
Top right: '>6/9 > 11/17' (first sign is a stray mark).
